entries.clue: Chubby harpist, Edenic resident – unearthly being, primarily! (6)

definitions.text: Chubby harpist, Edenic resident – unearthly being, primarily!

indicators.note: take each word's primary, i.e. first, letter

blocks.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

annotation.surface: A portrait of a plump little angel strumming a harp in paradise.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read straight it describes a cherub, and its six first letters spell one.
annotation.definitionFit: A cherub is the chubby winged angel of paintings, often shown with a harp in heaven.

entries.clue: Fruit, N. European, for Tom Sawyer’s pal (11,4)

blocks.note: a huckleberry is a small dark berry
a Finn comes from Finland, in northern Europe

annotation.surface: A list of foods and nationalities that turns into a question about Mark Twain.
annotation.walkthrough: The two parts sit in the clue in the same order as in the name.
annotation.definitionFit: Huckleberry Finn is Tom Sawyer's friend in Mark Twain's novels.

entries.clue: Ken Starr not quite liberal, extremely gross (7)

indicators.note: not the whole word: STARR loses its final letter
free and loose with the letters, so rearrange them

blocks.note: anagram fodder
STARR without its last letter

annotation.surface: A political jibe at Ken Starr, the US prosecutor who investigated Bill Clinton, as far from liberal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' reads as a political label for Starr; it is the instruction to rearrange KEN STAR.
annotation.definitionFit: Rankest is the superlative of rank, meaning gross or foul, so 'extremely gross'.

entries.clue: Bastille’s stormed, tougher than the rest (9)

indicators.note: a stormed fortress is broken open and its contents thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, apostrophe ignored

annotation.surface: A cry from the French Revolution, when the Bastille prison was stormed by the toughest of the mob.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in Bastille's is ignored, leaving nine letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Ballsy means gutsy or tough; the ballsiest is the toughest of all.

entries.clue: Tiny something taken by secretary (6)

blocks.note: an adjective for very small, said my-NEWT
a secretary takes notes of a meeting; one such note, said MIN-it

annotation.surface: An office scene where the secretary is handed some small item.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently, which hides the link: my-NEWT for tiny, MIN-it for the note.
annotation.definitionFit: Minute means tiny, and a secretary takes the minutes of a meeting.

entries.clue: Biblical lawgiver saunters with yen to depart (5)

indicators.note: to depart is to leave, so the yen leaves the word it sits in

blocks.note: to mosey is to stroll along
Y is the abbreviation for yen, the Japanese currency; it is removed from MOSEYS

annotation.surface: An Old Testament prophet ambling away with a longing to leave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yen' looks like a craving to be off; it is the currency's abbreviation Y, taken out of MOSEYS.
annotation.definitionFit: Moses received the Ten Commandments and gave the Law to the Israelites.

entries.clue: Book with the writer supporting N. African capital – not about Kenyan city (7)

indicators.note: in a down answer, what supports sits underneath, so B and I go below
remove C, the abbreviation for circa, 'about'

blocks.note: N = north(ern)
CAIRO without C (circa = about)
B = book
the writer refers to the setter: I

annotation.surface: A travel writer propping up a book about North African capitals.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is built bottom-up: B and I 'support' N and AIRO from below in the down light.
annotation.definitionFit: A city named by its country: Kenya's capital and largest city.

entries.clue: Inane, thick tot – he misbehaves – grin and bear it (4,2,2,3,4)

indicators.note: the letters behave badly and move out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: A harassed parent enduring a silly toddler's bad behaviour through gritted teeth.
annotation.walkthrough: The unkind description of the child is simply the letter supply; the parent's patience is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To take it on the chin is to accept a blow or setback without complaint.

entries.clue: Jack’s obstacle making Cedric and Les tickled in part (11)

indicators.note: the answer is only part of the run of words

blocks.note: cedriC AND LES TICKled

annotation.surface: Two men named Cedric and Les being tickled by a sailor's hurdle.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the nursery rhyme 'Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick'.
annotation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme, Jack has to jump over the candlestick.

entries.clue: Drug-addled greeting heard (4)

indicators.note: what is heard is the sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: hi is a greeting; say it aloud

annotation.surface: Someone stoned mumbling a hello.
annotation.walkthrough: HI and HIGH are spoken identically.
annotation.definitionFit: To be high is to be under the influence of drugs.

entries.clue: Tax riverside protection in announcement (4)

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken, so the word is taken by sound

blocks.note: a levee is an embankment against flooding

annotation.surface: A government announcing a charge to pay for flood defences.
annotation.walkthrough: A levee is a raised bank built along a river to stop it flooding; LEVEE and LEVY are said the same way.
annotation.definitionFit: A levy is a tax or charge imposed by an authority.

entries.clue: Everyman’s going to heads, having complaints (9)

blocks.note: the setter says 'I'll', short for I will
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Dungeness

annotation.surface: The setter off to see the bosses with a list of grievances.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heads' looks like bosses or the toilet; it means headlands, NESSES, a word seen in place names like Dungeness.
annotation.definitionFit: Complaint is the doctor's word for an ailment, the sense hidden behind the grumbling one the surface suggests.

entries.clue: Express view in ode to a Christmas tree? (5)

blocks.note: the poetic 'O' that opens an address in an ode
a pine is a typical Christmas tree

annotation.surface: A poet offering an opinion by way of a hymn to the festive tree, like the carol O Tannenbaum.
annotation.walkthrough: The ode would begin 'O pine!', the way an ode addresses its subject; run together it gives the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly formal: to put your opinion into words.

entries.clue: Slapdash, a bit, UEFA’s only partly regular (7)

indicators.note: the answer is a part of the words that precede it

blocks.note: slapdasH A BIT UEfa's

annotation.surface: A complaint that UEFA, European football's governing body, is careless and inconsistent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regular' looks like part of the complaint about UEFA; it is the definition, a regular customer.
annotation.definitionFit: A habitué is a frequent visitor to a place, a regular.

entries.clue: Leaves by swish old railway (7)

blocks.note: swish = stylish, chic
O = old
RY = railway

annotation.surface: Someone departing on a smart vintage train line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as a verb, departs; it is a noun, salad leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: Chicory is a plant grown for its bitter salad leaves.

entries.clue: Stop using smartphones, laptops etc? As if (4,3,2)

blocks.note: come off = give up; IT = information technology
both are scornful expressions of disbelief

annotation.surface: Advice to take a break from screens, met with a scoffing reply.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful reading: IT is information technology, and you come off it as you would a drug.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Come off it!' and 'As if!' both mean 'I don't believe you'.

entries.clue: Kind of tense? Ideal (7)

blocks.note: grammar names tenses: past, present, future, and the one for completed action, as in 'I have eaten'
an adjective: flawless, the best possible

annotation.walkthrough: The perfect is a grammatical tense for completed action; the second sense is the everyday one.
annotation.definitionFit: Perfect names a tense in grammar and also means ideal.

entries.clue: What the crossword setter sees as exquisite, friends! (4)

indicators.text: What the crossword setter sees as
indicators.note: the setter sees 'slap-up' as SLAP written going UP a down entry

blocks.note: slap-up = excellent, as in a slap-up meal; the UP is read as an instruction

annotation.surface: The setter gushing to solvers about something lovely.
annotation.walkthrough: Slap-up is British for lavish or first-rate. A setter reads 'SLAP up' literally: in a down entry, SLAP written upwards reads PALS.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: pal is informal English for a friend, suiting the setter's chummy 'friends!'.

entries.clue: Tangled dungarees abandoned by Dutch causes vexation (7)

indicators.note: knotted up, the letters jumbled
what is abandoned is left behind, so the Dutch abbreviation walks away from the word

blocks.note: overalls with a bib
Du. = Dutch; removed from DUNGAREES to leave NGAREES

annotation.surface: Someone infuriated by snarled-up work trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: Du. is the dictionary abbreviation for Dutch. Remove it from the front of DUNGAREES, then rearrange the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: To enrage is to make furious, to cause vexation.

entries.clue: Twerp in middle of heath finding track (7)

indicators.note: NIT goes into the middle of MOOR

blocks.note: a moor is open heathland; split MO|OR
nit = idiot

annotation.surface: A fool out on the heath who stumbles on a path.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Track' looks like a noun, a path on the heath; it is a verb, to follow closely.
annotation.definitionFit: To monitor something is to track it, keeping watch over it.

entries.clue: Taking home fishing kit (7)

blocks.note: take-home pay is what you earn after tax, i.e. your net pay
mesh used for nets

annotation.surface: An angler bringing their gear back after a trip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taking home' means pay after deductions, take-home pay, not carrying things home.
annotation.definitionFit: Netting is both clearing a sum as profit and the mesh fishermen use.

entries.clue: Schedule a hill to climb (4)

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading upwards

blocks.note: A as printed
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

annotation.surface: A walking itinerary with a hill to climb.
annotation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop in the West of England.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mainly British: a list setting out who takes which turn or duty.

entries.clue: Coat chicken? (5)

blocks.note: a coat of paint is one thickness spread over a surface
a hen kept for laying eggs; the question mark marks it as one example

annotation.surface: Instructions to coat a chicken, as in a recipe.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a cooking instruction; both words are nouns, a coat of paint and a laying hen.
annotation.definitionFit: A layer is a coating and also a hen that lays eggs.

entries.clue: King, extremely stuck up, beheaded: most awkward! (9)

indicators.note: a word's head is its first letter, so cutting it off removes the S

blocks.note: K = king, as in chess
SNOTTIEST without its first letter S

annotation.surface: A haughty king, loathed for his arrogance, is executed.
annotation.walkthrough: Snotty means snobbish, so 'extremely stuck up' is SNOTTIEST before its head comes off.
annotation.definitionFit: A knotty problem is a tricky one; the knottiest is the most awkward.

entries.clue: Merry after skipping starter: broken bread in Scandinavia (5)

indicators.note: tipsy and unsteady, so the letters reel about
BROKEN loses its first letter

blocks.note: BROKEN without its first letter B

annotation.surface: A cheerful diner who skipped the first course breaking bread on a Nordic trip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is slang for money, so the definition is a currency. 'Merry' starts the clue looking like a mood; it tells you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: The krone is the currency of Denmark and Norway, and bread is slang for money.

entries.clue: Oath: if doing, perform honestly (2,4,5)

indicators.note: the letters perform, putting on a new arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: A sworn promise to act with integrity if called upon.
annotation.walkthrough: The oath theme fits the answer nicely, but 'Oath' is fodder, not the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To act in good faith is to act honestly, without intent to deceive.

entries.clue: For himself, the king’s – that is to say – casual apparel (6)

blocks.note: a king speaking of his own things says 'one's'
i.e. = id est, that is

annotation.surface: A monarch, speaking of his own wardrobe, describes his loungewear.
annotation.walkthrough: Royals traditionally say 'one' for 'I', so the king's word for 'my' is ONE'S.
annotation.definitionFit: A onesie is a loose all-in-one garment worn for lounging.

entries.clue: Cheers! Drink, then eastern casserole (6)

blocks.note: ta = thanks, as is cheers in British speech
gin = a drink
surface padding: the next piece follows on
E = eastern

annotation.surface: A toast, a drink, and then a spicy stew from the East for dinner.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain 'Cheers!' and 'Ta!' both mean thanks, not only a toast.
annotation.definitionFit: A tagine is a slow-cooked North African stew, named after its pot.
